claims.text: At elevated temperature, reactive phases in the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy form a transient protective oxide scale.
Mechanical wear continuously removes the protective oxide scale.
Removal of the oxide exposes phases that are highly susceptible to rapid corrosion.
Cyclic oxide formation and removal produces a synergistic interaction between wear and corrosion.
The wear-corrosion synergy accelerates total degradation relative to wear or corrosion acting alone.
The alloy initially has well-defined phase boundaries and a pristine surface without significant pre-formed oxide.
Temperatures above approximately 500°C are sufficient to promote oxidation under the proposed conditions.
Microstructural phase boundaries govern differential oxidation and wear resistance.
Elevated temperature facilitates in-situ formation of the protective oxide.
Repeated oxide removal exposes fresh metal surfaces that undergo rapid corrosion.
The combined degradation is greater than the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion contributions.
The oxide scale may temporarily reduce the wear rate.
Oxide removal causes spikes in corrosion rate immediately after wear events.
The proposed mechanism requires a temperature high enough for continuing oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism requires mechanical loading sufficient to disrupt the oxide continuously.
The mechanism may not operate when either oxide formation or mechanically driven oxide disruption is absent.
Phase-specific oxidation and wear dynamics have not been directly established for this particular alloy.
